extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, sociology, and history; readers of classical social theory
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and formulating general laws of social order and social progress (social statics and social dynamics), including requisites of stable political union and methods for deriving empirical and a priori sociological laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Statics: relational analysis of social elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Each element of the social state "shall be always and exclusively considered relatively to all the other elements, with the whole of which it is united by mutual interdependence." Social Statics infers the characteristic marks of one mode of social existence from others, analogous to anatomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relations among contemporaneous social phenomena to infer conditions where direct observation is impracticable; avoid treating elements independently or absolutely; treat elements only in their mutual relations. Watch for over-simplification: necessary relations are not so simple or precise that results could only arise from a single coordination—estimate limits of variation to avoid error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual interdependence and transmission of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Every social element has connections, often immediate, with other elements; changes in one part operate immediately or very speedily upon the rest—"the communication of motion from one object to another proves a connection between them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a social phenomenon, trace likely propagated effects across institutions, sciences, and arts; account for reciprocity between nations and weakening of consensus with diminishing affinity or contact. Avoid analyses that ignore indirect or distant dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between form of government and state of civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a necessary correlation between the form of government existing in any society and the contemporaneous state of civilization; abstract debates about government forms in isolation are largely fruitless without this correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories of government by examining them in relation to the actual state of civilization; use comparative historical evidence to ground claims about suitability or consequences of government forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites of a State / stable political union (institutional minimums)
rubrics_metrics.description: No numerous society has been held together without laws or equivalent usages; without tribunals and an organized force to execute decisions; without public authorities whom the community obeyed or were generally bound to obey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a society constitutes a State or can maintain collective existence, check for the presence and functioning of laws/usages, tribunals, enforcement mechanisms, and generally recognized authorities. The absence of these correlates with dissolution or reconstruction on a new basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of education with restraining discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of education for citizens, beginning in infancy and continued through life, whose main and incessant ingredient is restraining discipline: training to subordinate personal impulses to the ends of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political stability by the extent and strictness of civic education and disciplining institutions; relaxation of restraining discipline tends toward internal disorganization, selfish conflict, and decline. Consider how civil and military policies or religious teaching perform this function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling of allegiance or loyalty (fixed point)
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary condition is the existence of a feeling of allegiance or loyalty—some settled, permanent thing in the constitution of the state (gods, persons, laws, liberties, or principles) regarded as secure against disturbance and beyond practical challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for a shared, sacralized, or generally accepted "fixed point" in a polity that preserves fundamental principles during disputes. If fundamental principles are habitually questioned, the state risks persistent internal dissension or civil war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of cohesion (sympathy, common interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stability requires a strong active principle of cohesion among members: a feeling of common interest (sympathy, union), not nationalism in the vulgar sense; parts of the community must not regard one another as foreigners but as one people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate national unity by degrees of mutual sympathy and shared interest across regions and groups. Differentiate healthy cohesion from hostile/narrow nationalism; absence of cohesion explains fragmentation and susceptibility to foreign domination or internal separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Dynamics: tracing sequences and filiation of social states
rubrics_metrics.description: Social Dynamics focuses on the successive order—observing and explaining the sequences of social conditions; the aim is to trace leading general circumstances of each generation to causes in the immediately preceding generation (the filiation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To explain social change, prioritize proximate antecedents and establish derivative laws by examining immediate causal chains between successive social states. Recognize that the whole often produces the whole in filiation; thus derive 'axiomata media' governing generation of social states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine statical and dynamical views to derive correspondence laws
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to combine the statical view (contemporaneous conditions) with the dynamical (progressive changes) to obtain empirical laws of correspondence between simultaneous states and simultaneous changes of social elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming sociological laws, empirically verify correspondences both among coexistent elements and among their simultaneous changes over time. Purely fragmentary progressive observations are insufficient; joint analysis yields better derivative laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predominant social agent: state of speculative faculties (beliefs and knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: One social element is pre-eminent among agents of social progression: the state of the speculative faculties of mankind (the nature of beliefs and knowledge). The progress of knowledge determines industrial, artistic, moral, and political progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In causal accounts of social change, treat transformations in beliefs, knowledge, and prevailing opinions as central causal factors that enable or limit other improvements; assess how shifts in intellectual convictions precede and precipitate broader social change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of long-term historical scope and a priori grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Because changes in knowledge and opinions are slow and manifest only over long intervals, determining laws of sequence requires considering the whole past; empirical laws should then be converted into scientific theorems by deduction a priori from principles of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drawing strong sequence laws from narrowly spaced historical samples; seek wide temporal coverage and attempt to deduce observed regularities from fundamental principles of human nature for scientific generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comte's law of three stages (progress of human knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculation on every subject passes through three stages: (1) explanation by supernatural agencies, (2) by metaphysical abstractions, and (3) the final state of ascertaining laws of succession and similitude (positive science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite schema as a heuristic for interpreting historical changes in modes of explanation and their social consequences; check concurrence of historical facts with probabilities from human mental constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of empirical generalizations (need for intermediate principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws generalized from history often remain too far from elementary laws of human nature because many intervening links and concurrent causes exist; such results are evidence toward, but not substitutes for, 'middle principles' (axiomata media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat broad empirical tendencies (e.g., increasing primacy of mental qualities over bodily ones) as provisional; aim to identify intermediate principles that explain how elementary human nature yields observed historical regularities. Be cautious of over-generalizing without these mediating laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical regularity en masse as evidence for causation in human actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate regularities in recorded social phenomena (e.g., murders, suicides, undirected letters) show striking constancy year-to-year, suggesting that human volitions conform to laws of causation when seen en masse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistical aggregates to test hypotheses about causal laws in social behavior: consistent proportions across time support the causal interpretation. Understand that individual unpredictability does not invalidate aggregate regularity; account for known sources of general perturbations (policy changes, public events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of causation of human actions (compatibility with historical laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human actions are joint results of general laws/circumstances (state of civilization) and particular individual causes (temperament, upbringing, associations); if this causation principle holds for individuals, it must hold for collective man and history will be subject to scientific laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting predictability or lawfulness in history, ground arguments in the dual-cause model and employ empirical verification (statistics, registers) to confirm that aggregate outcomes approximate constant quantities under stable general conditions. Address objections rooted in free-will by clarifying that causation does not imply fatalism but lawful regularity.
